splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of defendants. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively expand criminal liability through interpretive commentary rather than through formal lawmaking.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expanded the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid, deferrable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the guideline text. This affects thousands of federal sentences because many prior drug convictions are for conspiracy.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor, so inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is disqualifying. This split produces dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on the circuit, with some avoiding mandatory minimums and others not.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' effectively means 'or,' so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such relief exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory stacked § 924(c) sentences, can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold such changes can never be extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others allow consideration of changes in law. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment attempting to authorize such relief has intensified the split.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in saying otherwise.

positions.label: Changes in law may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, either alone or combined with other factors, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement authorizing such consideration is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the career-offender guideline's reference to 'an offense under federal or state law' requires the substance at issue to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects the base offense level and career-offender status of many defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-controlled substances suffice
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include any offense under state law, with no requirement that the substance also be federally controlled.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge Bureau of Prisons decisions regarding conditions or terms of confinement (such as First Step Act earned time credits) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) are also available.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoner challenges to conditions of confinement or whether such challenges may also proceed as civil rights actions. The split has deepened in the context of First Step Act implementation, where prisoners challenge BOP decisions about earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is not exclusive for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement (as opposed to fact or duration of confinement) may be brought as civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas corpus.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge effectively seeks speedier release (including challenges to BOP earned time credit calculations), habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the petition date and the conversion date belongs to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This matters significantly for homeowners who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 during periods of rising real estate values.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, policies, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences that punish defendants for violations of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to facilitating the defendant's reentry into the community.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of sentences imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to punish for supervised release violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must be aimed at reentry and rehabilitation rather than punishment for the violation itself.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is impermissible — reentry focus required
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be focused on the defendant's reentry into the community and may not be imposed as punishment for the supervised release violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is governed by the civil timeline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). This determines whether many fee-award appeals are timely filed.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case and the shorter criminal appeal deadline governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing requirements for actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing of when assumptions can be selected directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions for withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select or adjust actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans flexibility in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered supervision beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, so the release term does not run while the supervisee is a fugitive.

positions.label: No tolling — term runs regardless
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms during absconding, so the term continues to run and expires as scheduled.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any previously presented claim even if they satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the (b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements and are not subject to the additional (b)(1) categorical bar on previously presented claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standard for evaluating whether candidates have pre-election standing to challenge voting and ballot-counting rules. The resolution of this issue determines whether election rule challenges must wait until after an election (when remedies may be impractical) or can be brought proactively, with major implications for mail-in voting and ballot counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules that allegedly dilute or impair lawful votes.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates cannot demonstrate a sufficiently concrete and particularized injury from election rules to satisfy Article III standing requirements before an election occurs.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have not uniformly addressed whether denial of a sealing motion for medical records qualifies as a collateral order. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review, but other circuits may not extend the collateral order doctrine this far, creating potential divergence in the availability of interlocutory appeal for privacy-related sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable as collateral order
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders, even those involving medical privacy, do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements for immediate appeal because privacy interests can be adequately vindicated through other means.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
